Valve nerfed the firing accuracy
for three person stacks and beyond.
thus nixing Stacking and casting this mechanic—
a hallmark of teamwork and the game itself— into the grave.
So today, let’s briefly chat about
why boosts and Stacking are popular,
and why they give map designers such headaches.
From one point six Nuke’s five man stack plant
to Olofmeister’s infamous Overpass boost.
and up to Valve recently patching that gap
in Ancient’s mid wall,
we can see that having folks stack up
like that DOES impact game balance.
Players found that standing tall
truly let them see far, turning
many once overlooked bits of cover into potent info
gathering spots and pick off spots.
And THAT’s why players love boosting and Stacking!
First, its rich tactical depth
lets teams glean more intel, craft unconventional crossfires,
and devise unique utility combos.
And that’s what players want to see.
We want to see pro players on stage
winning with unforeseen tactics, and simple team plays
yielding lethal results.
While these moves might not be all that balanced,
they undeniably enriched the gameplay,
boosted match spectacle, and spawned tons of iconic moments.
Like that twenty twenty one
Stockholm match—TYLOO versus Spirit’s four stack.
This tournament’s teamwork
truly gave us many shocks—TYLOO is no longer
just a dry push squad!
but they only scored three points that game.
Such boosts and Stacking—fun to watch,
sure, but unbalanced, too.
This forced designers, when crafting maps,
to factor in second, third, or even fourth layers of height.
Let’s rewind to the one point six era.
Counter intuitively, back in an era
when both PC power and game tactics were scarce,
Map designers quite like to keep some boost spots,
like V I P on Inferno.
Mirage’s jump up and V I P.
All are spots you need a boost to reach.
but this also spawned a new issue:
it vastly limited a solo player’s room to shine.
since you need at least two folks
to snag the keys to these routes.
So now, Valve picked a near perfect way to tweak things.
While they tweaked these spots
so one person could get up there,
they also gave boosts a chance to shine.
Such as Mirage’s and Town’s V I P spots—via a boost,
you can access them silently.
catching the enemy off guard.
But! Let’s head back to one point six.
Back then, map design
was still quite crude—since most maps had
walls as walls
and paths as paths,
the high ground areas weren’t designed all that precisely.
which let players “Stacking” to snag a non pre aimed spot.

Now, map designers have learned their lesson.
They’d specifically craft the heights of crates,
low walls, jump pads, and other cover
to prevent boosters from gaining undue advantages,
and would add plenty of anti boost designs.
Maps will feature various ceilings,
crossbeams, trees, and such
to constrain players
and stop them from gaining unusual sightlines via Stacking.
So, sadly, designers started telling players HOW to play.
Once players pulled off a boost or Stacking
that designers didn’t foresee,
they’d swiftly patch and scrap that spot.
But since Stacking was so hard to predict,
they just stopped allowing it outright;
in CS:GO, for instance, a three man stack would be unstable,
and players would slowly slide off to one side.
More drastically, on the twenty third of march ,
twenty twenty three,
when CS two testing kicked off,
players in stacks of three or more
were barred from firing outright.
But that change was so damn dumb it sparked player backlash,
so it got scrapped on the seventh of june of that same year.
All in all,
while designers have kept limiting Stacking to curb fairness
debates in matches,
this trait has long since become part of CS’s unique culture.
So, while they shut one door, they opened a window.
They allowed boosts to exist,
letting players pull off neat plays
with just a simple two person team up.
And this, in turn, spurred on map design evolution—spots
like the stables on Town,
those dual, opposing boost spots on Amusement Park,
and the newly tweaked mid gate on Anubis.
Even more so, smoke grenades spread to a height
that lets those on a boost spot folks behind it.
You could say the boost made CS map design
shift from “how tall is one player?”
to “how tall are TWO players?”
And these wondrous chemical reactions
make up the charm of teamwork,
giving CS its depth and making it worth mastering.
but in the end, I gotta say,
Valve’s change was SO fucking trash—taking away
Stacking like that!
something that GREATLY boosts match spectacle—gone!
Just plain bonkers!
